::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}
A correct regression calculation can support an incorrect research claim.
This chapter connects adjustment, composition, selection, measurement and
dependence with the comparison each analysis actually makes. Generated
studies reveal mechanisms with known truth; Berkeley admissions,
occupation records and Project STAR show what the same questions mean in
real evidence. By the end, you can choose an estimand, explain when
adjustment helps or harms, recognize a change of unit or population, and
write a claim that respects the design and the uncertainty. The chapter
teaches how to audit a claim; it introduces causal-design vocabulary
without supplying an advanced causal estimator.
:::

In the autumn of 1973 the six largest graduate departments at the
University of California, Berkeley, returned decisions to 4,526
applicants. Among the 2,691 men, 1,198 were admitted, a rate of
44.5188 percent; among the 1,835 women, 557 were admitted, a rate of
30.3542 percent. A gap of 14.1645 percentage points on more than four
thousand decisions is not a rounding artifact, and a logistic
regression of admission on applicant gender returns a coefficient
many standard errors from zero. Now add one column that was in the
file all along: the department applied to. Four of the six
departments admitted women at a higher rate than men, the two
exceptions differed little, and the same regression with department
included moves the gender coefficient to the other side of zero with
an interval that comfortably contains equality. Both calculations are
correct, and they are not contradictory, because they answer
different questions: one describes the applicant pool as it was
composed, in which men and women applied to very differently
selective departments, and the other describes applicants within a
department. Neither is by itself an account of how the decisions were
made; the original authors said so explicitly [@bickel1975]. This
chapter is about the distance between a number that is correct and a
claim that is credible: what comparison did this model make, who was
in it, what was measured, how many analyses were tried, and does the
final sentence describe that comparison or a more attractive one?

## Credibility Is Alignment {#ch14-alignment}

### Six commitments that must line up

A quantitative claim rests on a chain of commitments and is credible
only when they agree. The failures in this chapter are misalignments,
not computational errors: the regression runs, the standard errors
print, and nothing in the output announces that the quantity named in
the introduction and the quantity the model computed differ.

| Element | Question it answers |
|:--|:--|
| Research question | What do we want to know, and in what mode: descriptive, associational, predictive, or causal? |
| Estimand | What quantity, for which units and conditions, would answer that question? |
| Design | How were units produced, selected, observed, assigned, and retained? |
| Data | Which rows and columns survive into the analysis, and what do they measure? |
| Model | What comparison does the fitted specification actually compute? |
| Claim | What sentence is written at the end, and how far does it reach? |

: The six commitments behind a credible claim. {#tbl-ch14-commitments tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Three habits keep them aligned, and none of them is a diagnostic plot.
Name the estimand in words before fitting anything [@lundberg2021].
Describe the comparison the model makes in one sentence that names the
unit, the contrast, and what is held fixed. Then check that the
concluding sentence uses no verb the design cannot support.

### Pooled, within-group, and between-group comparisons

Let $Y$ be an outcome, $X$ a focal predictor, and $Z$ a grouping or
adjustment variable. Three quantities recur in this chapter and are
different: pooling mixes groups, conditioning compares within them,
and aggregation makes the groups themselves the rows.

$$
\Delta\mu_{\mathrm{pooled}}=E(Y\mid X=x+1)-E(Y\mid X=x),
$$

$$
\Delta\mu_{\mathrm{within}}(z)=E(Y\mid X=x+1, Z=z)-E(Y\mid X=x, Z=z),
$$

$$
\Delta\mu_{\mathrm{between}}=E(\bar Y_z\mid \bar X_z=x+1)
-E(\bar Y_z\mid \bar X_z=x).
$$

The first averages over whatever mixture of $Z$ the data contain. The
second removes that mixture, and an additive regression including $Z$
estimates a common value when the stratum-specific comparisons are
similar. The third changes the unit of analysis, since its rows are
groups, and can take any sign relative to the other two. Section 3.3
adds a fourth, the **standardized** comparison, which reweights the
stratum-specific comparisons by a declared common distribution of $Z$.

A **strict Simpson reversal** occurs when the pooled comparison and
every stratified comparison point in opposite directions [@simpson1951;
@yule1903]. The broader **aggregation reversal** also covers a sign
change between a pooled comparison and an adjusted or standardized
summary when the stratum-specific comparisons are heterogeneous. Nothing
paradoxical has happened: composition changes the weights and, usually,
the quantity estimated. Section 3.1's tutoring reversal is strict;
Section 3.3's Berkeley reversal is the broader kind.

### Four modes of claim and their verbs

Chapters 1 and 7 introduced the typology of questions. It returns here
as the vocabulary of the final audit, because most overclaiming is a
silent change of mode between the analysis and the conclusion.

| Mode | Legitimate verbs | What the design must supply |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Descriptive | is, was, differed, ranged | A defined population and unit, and data that represent them |
| Associational | is associated with, differs by, tends to be higher among | Defined units, measurements, conditioning set and observed support |
| Predictive | predicts, forecasts, is expected to be | Predictors available at the intended decision time and an honest held-out performance estimate for the named deployment population (Chapter 13) [@shmueli2010] |
| Causal | causes, raises, reduces, would change | A defined intervention and target population, with assignment or an identification argument under explicit, defensible assumptions [@shadish2002] |

: Four modes of claim, their verbs, and what each requires. {#tbl-ch14-modes tbl-colwidths="[14,30,56]"}

The verbs are not decoration. "Pupils who received more tutoring
scored lower" and "tutoring lowered scores" are different claims, and
the same regression output can be made to look like support for
either. A reader who has only the output cannot tell which claim was
intended; a reader who has the estimand, the design and the
conditioning set can.

## Adjustment: Confounders, Mediators, and Colliders {#ch14-adjustment}

### A diagram records assumptions

To decide whether conditioning on $Z$ helps, something must be assumed
about how $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ were produced. The minimum vocabulary is
three structures, drawn as a **directed acyclic graph**: an arrow means
"is a direct cause of", and no directed path returns to its starting point
[@pearl2009]. A **confounder** $Z$ causes both $X$ and $Y$, so leaving
it out mixes the direct path with the back-door path through $Z$ and
adjusting removes that mixture. A **mediator** $M$ lies on a causal path from $X$ to $Y$, so
conditioning on it blocks that pathway in a total-effect comparison.
A mediator is one kind of **post-treatment variable**. The broader term
also includes consequences of treatment that do not mediate its effect,
including the collider in the next example; timing alone does not
identify a variable's causal role. A
**collider** $C$ is caused by both $X$ and an unmeasured $U$ that also
causes $Y$; the path through $C$ is blocked while $C$ is left alone, and
conditioning on it opens that path, creating an $X$-$U$ association that
did not exist [@elwert2014]. The practical rule reverses "adjust for
everything available": choose the adjustment set for the stated estimand
from an explicit structure. Pre-treatment common causes are usually
needed; for a total-effect target, mediators and colliders are not.
Timing rules out some roles without settling any
[@vanderweele2019; @pearl2009], which is why measurement timing and
the assumed structure belong in the data audit.

A diagram of this kind records assumptions. It is not evidence, it is
not produced by the data, and drawing one does not make an

adjustment decision arguable in public: a reader can dispute an
arrow, and cannot dispute an unstated intuition.
:::

### Adjusting for a mediator on a randomized programme






Both examples in this section randomize assignment. The particular
post-treatment variables considered here change or distort the total-effect
comparison; this is not a claim that adjustment for baseline predictors
is harmful in randomized studies. A
district randomizes 600 pupils to a study-skills programme, which raises
homework completion, which raises achievement; a direct pathway does not
run through homework.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{program}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(.5),\\
\text{homework}_i &= 6+2\,\text{program}_i+u_i,
&& u_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 2^2),\\
\text{achievement}_i &= 50+3\,\text{program}_i
+2.5\,\text{homework}_i+\varepsilon_i,
&& \varepsilon_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 5^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

The total effect is the direct path plus the indirect path,
$3+2.5\times2=8$ points; the direct effect, holding homework
fixed, is 3. These are two estimands, and the question decides which
matters: a district deciding whether to fund the programme wants the
total effect. With seed 14007 the unadjusted regression gives 8.0198
[6.8566, 9.1830] and the regression adding homework gives 3.066
[2.1023, 4.0297]. Both are correct. If the report asks whether the
programme raises achievement and by how much, the adjusted model answers
a question nobody asked and understates the total by more than half.
Nothing in the coefficient table warns of this; the clue is temporal,
because homework completion follows randomization and is a consequence
of the programme.

::: {.callout-warning title="The most common version of this mistake"}
"We controlled for baseline motivation, homework, attendance and
engagement to isolate the effect of the programme." If the programme
changed any of those variables, they are post-treatment and the
resulting coefficient is not the programme's total effect. Adding
covariates is not automatically conservative.
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lm(achievement ~ program, data = med)
lm(achievement ~ program + homework, data = med)
```
:::





**Change one assumption: family support also affects homework and achievement.**
The original recipe makes the homework and achievement disturbances
independent. Now keep its 600 assignments and both error draws, and add
an independent pre-programme support variable $S_i\sim\mathrm{Normal}(0,1)$,
drawn under seed 14016:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{homework}_i &= 6+2\,\text{program}_i+2S_i+u_i,\\
\text{achievement}_i &= 50+3\,\text{program}_i+
  2.5\,\text{homework}_i+4S_i+\varepsilon_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

The programme still has total effect 8 and direct effect 3 in this
generated process. Before looking at the estimates, predict which
comparison remains supported by random assignment. Assignment makes
programme independent of support, but it does not randomize homework.
Among pupils with the same homework amount, programme participation can
go together with less support; support also affects achievement.
Holding homework fixed therefore opens a noncausal path unless support
is adequately controlled.

### Adjusting for a collider on the same programme








Now the third variable is caused by two things at once. The same
randomized programme runs; unmeasured family support raises achievement;
and both programme participation and family support make a high score on
an optional end-of-year portfolio more likely. The portfolio score is
recorded and looks like a sensible covariate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{program}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(.5),
&&\text{support}_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 1),\\
\text{achievement}_i &= 50+4\,\text{program}_i
+5\,\text{support}_i+\varepsilon_i,
&& \varepsilon_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 4^2),\\
\text{portfolio}_i &= 1\,\text{program}_i+1\,\text{support}_i+\nu_i,
&& \nu_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 0.7^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

With seed 14069 the unadjusted estimate is 4.1052 [3.0316, 5.1788],
close to the true 4 because randomization made programme and support
independent. Adjusting for the portfolio score gives 0.1726 [$-0.6755$,
1.0206]: the whole comparison vanishes, and a researcher reading only
that model would report a null. Adjusting instead for the true cause
gives 4.0396 [3.4011, 4.6781]. The mechanism is visible directly. In the
whole sample the correlation between programme and support is .0061; in
the lower, middle and upper thirds of the portfolio distribution, each
of 200 records, it is $-.4106$, $-.4978$ and $-.2240$, because a high
portfolio score can be reached either through the programme or through
family support. Conditioning manufactured an association the design had
eliminated, and because support also causes achievement, that
manufactured association contaminates the programme coefficient
[@elwert2014].

### An adjustment decision table

\Needspace{30\baselineskip}

| Role of the candidate variable | Timing relative to the focal predictor | Adjust? | Consequence of adjusting |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Common cause of predictor and outcome (confounder) | Before | Include in a sufficient causal adjustment set | Blocks the represented back-door path under the assumed structure and a suitable model |
| Cause of the outcome only, unrelated to the predictor | Before | Optional | No systematic change; can improve precision |
| Consequence of the predictor on the path to the outcome (mediator) | After | No, for a total-effect target | Changes the target to a conditional comparison; a direct causal reading needs additional conditions |
| Consequence of both the predictor and an outcome cause (collider) | After | No | Creates an association that did not exist; can reverse or nullify the estimate |
| Consequence of the outcome | After | No | Selects on information about the outcome; the conditional comparison no longer answers the original causal target |
| Proxy measured with substantial error | Before | Partially useful | Leaves residual confounding; see Section 5.1 |

: What adjusting for a candidate variable does, by its assumed role. {#tbl-ch14-adjustment tbl-colwidths="[30,18,14,38]"}

The direct-effect reading in the mediator row requires a suitable model
and control of mediator--outcome confounding; randomization of the programme
alone does not establish it. The generated linear recipe supplies those
conditions. A sufficient adjustment set blocks the relevant back-door
paths without opening another path; merely including one plausible common
cause need not remove all confounding.

The table summarizes assumptions; it is not a test. No procedure applied
to the observed data classifies a variable into these rows, because
every row can produce the same coefficient movement. Timing, substantive
theory and documented measurement are what distinguish them.

::: {.callout-warning title="A coefficient that changes is not a diagnosis"}
Adding $Z$ moved the focal coefficient from 0.9 to 0.2. That is
compatible with $Z$ being a confounder whose removal was necessary, a
mediator whose inclusion destroyed the target, a collider whose
inclusion introduced bias, or a variable so strongly related to $X$
that the movement is sampling noise on an imprecise estimate.
Reporting the movement is useful; reading it as evidence of
confounding is not warranted by the movement alone.
:::

## Reversals and Simpson's Paradox {#ch14-reversals}

### A reversal built on purpose






A generated example is preferable here because the comparison structure
is known and can be altered deliberately. A district records, for every
pupil, weekly hours of supplementary tutoring and an end-of-year reading
score. Better-resourced schools offer more tutoring on average and also
have higher average scores for reasons unrelated to tutoring, while
within any one school tutoring goes to pupils who are struggling, so
pupils receiving more tutoring tend to score lower.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{hours}_{ig} &= \mu_g+u_{ig},
&& u_{ig}\sim\text{Normal}(0, 0.7^2),\\
\text{score}_{ig} &= \alpha_g+\beta_W(\text{hours}_{ig}-\mu_g)
+\varepsilon_{ig},
&& \varepsilon_{ig}\sim\text{Normal}(0, 4^2),
\end{aligned}
$$

with school means $\mu_g\in\{1.5, 3, 4.5, 6\}$ hours, baselines
$\alpha_g\in\{30, 42, 54, 66\}$ points, a true within-school slope
$\beta_W=-1.6$, and 60 pupils per school. Seed 14001 gives school mean
hours 1.4945, 3.0833, 4.3461 and 6.1030 with mean scores 29.7655,
42.1576, 54.1161 and 65.3627. In @fig-ch14-reversal, four
clouds march up and to the right, and inside each cloud the trend runs
down and to the right. A model that never sees the school label can only
summarize the march.

### Three fits, three estimands




















Fit the three models and put their values beside the recipe. The pooled
slope is 6.5784 [6.0565, 7.1003] with $R^2=.7215$; the school-adjusted
slope is $-2.0018$ [$-2.8533$, $-1.1504$], covering the true $-1.6$; the
between-school slope, from four rows and 2 residual df, is 7.8372
[6.0877, 9.5866]. Only one estimates the parameter in the recipe. The
other two correctly estimate how score and tutoring covary in the
district as composed and how school averages covary; both would be wrong
as answers to a question about pupils inside a school.

With groups $g=1,\dots,G$ and
the within and between sums of squares and cross-products
$S_{xx}^{W}=\sum_g\sum_{i\in g}(x_{ig}-\bar x_g)^2$ and
$S_{xx}^{B}=\sum_g n_g(\bar x_g-\bar x)^2$, and $S_{xy}^{W}$, $S_{xy}^{B}$
defined the same way, the totals split as $S_{xx}=S_{xx}^{W}+S_{xx}^{B}$
and $S_{xy}=S_{xy}^{W}+S_{xy}^{B}$, so

$$
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{pooled}}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}
=w_W\widehat\beta_W+w_B\widehat\beta_B,\qquad
w_W=\frac{S_{xx}^{W}}{S_{xx}},\quad w_B=\frac{S_{xx}^{B}}{S_{xx}}.
$$

The pooled slope is a weighted average of a within-group and a
between-group slope, weighted by the shares of predictor variation
inside and between groups; the weights are non-negative and sum to one,
and the slopes they combine are unrestricted. Here $S_{xx}^{W}=100.5503$
and $S_{xx}^{B}=685.3977$ of a total 785.948, so $w_W=.1279$ and
$w_B=.8721$: only about an eighth of the predictor variation lies inside
schools, the weighted average returns the fitted 6.5784 at full
precision, and the pooled slope is dominated by a comparison of school
averages. Make the schools more alike in average tutoring and $w_B$
shrinks; make them more different and it grows. Composition is a
property of the sample, not of the phenomenon, so the reversal can be
created or removed while the within-school association stays fixed. This
recipe specifies an observed joint distribution, not the effect of
intervening on tutoring. Appendix A gives
the derivation and its categorical counterpart.

|:--|:--|:--|--:|
| Across this district's pupils, how do reading scores compare between those receiving more and fewer tutoring hours? | Pooled | `score ~ hours` | 6.5784 |
| Among pupils at the same school, how do scores compare between those receiving more and fewer hours? | Within-group | `score ~ hours + school` | $-2.0018$ |
| Do schools that provide more tutoring on average have higher average scores? | Between-group, school as unit | mean score on mean hours | 7.8372 |

Take each school separately before accepting one adjusted number. The
four school-specific slopes are $-2.1063$ [$-4.0928$, $-0.1197$],
$-1.8864$ [$-3.3807$, $-0.3920$], $-1.2688$ [$-3.0443$, 0.5067] and
$-2.6281$ [$-4.3226$, $-0.9335$]: all negative, one interval covering
zero. The additive model reports a single precision-weighted summary of
those four, which is useful when they are similar and misleading when
they are not; Chapter 10 supplies the check, and the `hours:school`
product block here gives $F(3,232)=0.4345$, $p=.7285$, unsurprisingly,
because the recipe gave all four schools the same slope. Subtracting
each school's mean from `hours` removes all between-school variation in
the predictor, and an ordinary regression on that centred predictor
reproduces $-2.0018$ exactly, without any group indicator.

Everything above comes from `lm()` on clearly defined rows. The
within-between distinction is the entry point to multilevel and linear
mixed models, which are outside this collection; Section 6.3 explains
why ordinary standard errors from a pooled fit on clustered data need
care.

### Berkeley admissions: the same arithmetic on a census




























The best-known reversal in the social sciences is a two-by-two-by-six
table of graduate admissions decisions, a good empirical case because

### One adjusted number needs checking

The additive model is itself an assumption and deserves the scrutiny the
pooled model gets. Comparing it with the model that lets the odds ratio
vary gives a likelihood-ratio deviance of 20.2043 on 5 df, $p=.0011$;
the department-specific odds ratios run from 0.8186 in E to 2.8636 in A,
and A is the main source of the departure, admitting 82.4074 percent of
its 108 female applicants against 62.0606 percent of its 825 male ones.
The adjusted number that reverses the pooled result is therefore itself
a summary the data do not fully support.

::: {.callout-warning title="A reversal is a descriptive fact, not an explanation"}
The table shows that a pooled and a department-conditional comparison
point in opposite directions. It does not show why women and men
applied where they did, whether departmental capacity and funding were
themselves shaped by the fields women entered, or whether any
individual decision was fair. @bickel1975 were explicit that their
analysis concerned the aggregation, and that no bias within
departments is compatible with disadvantage arising earlier, in the
processes that channel applicants toward differently funded fields.
For that broader question department is a mediator, not a confounder,
and conditioning on it removes exactly the pathway the question is
about. Neither comparison answers whether the process was fair.
:::

## Selection, Support, and Regression to the Mean {#ch14-selection}

Adjustment changes what is held fixed. Selection changes who is in the
comparison at all, and it operates before any model is fitted.

### Regression toward the mean after selection on a noisy baseline
















In standard units a regression line predicts $\widehat z_y=r\,z_x$.
When $0<r<1$, its prediction for an extreme first value is nearer the
mean on the second measurement. The spread of individual second
measurements remains: the whole population does not converge on its
mean. Here that distinction reveals why a before--after comparison can
mislead when entry depends on a noisy baseline.

Suppose 400 pupils take a reading test, the lowest-scoring 15 percent
enter a support programme, and they are retested at the end of the year.
Their average score rises substantially, and the obvious reading is that
the programme worked. The recipe below contains no programme effect at
all.

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_i &\sim\text{Normal}(50, 8^2)
&&\text{(stable ability, unobserved)},\\
\text{pretest}_i &= T_i+\varepsilon_{i1},
&& \varepsilon_{i1}\sim\text{Normal}(0, 6^2),\\
\text{posttest}_i &= T_i+\varepsilon_{i2},
&& \varepsilon_{i2}\sim\text{Normal}(0, 6^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Both measurements are the same stable quantity plus independent noise,
so the correlation between them, the reliability under this model, is
$8^2/(8^2+6^2)=.64$; with seed 14002 the observed correlation is
.6371. Selecting the lowest scorers on the pretest selects pupils with
genuinely low ability **and** pupils whose measurement error happened to
be negative, and the second group cannot repeat that luck
[@galton1886; @barnett2005]. The 60 selected pupils, all below
38.3371, average 33.5726 on the pretest and 39.0568 on the posttest, a
gain of 5.4842 points with a paired $t(59)=4.8378$, $p<.0001$ and a
95 percent interval of [3.2158, 7.7526]. Every number is computed
correctly, and the effect written into the recipe is zero. The mirror
image confirms the mechanism: the highest 15 percent show an apparent
decline of $-5.823$.

A bigger sample does not repair this: the phenomenon is systematic, and
more pupils estimate the spurious gain more precisely. A comparison
group selected the same way does repair it, because both arms are then
subject to identical regression to the mean. Keep the 60 selected pupils
in their original row order rather than sorting them by pretest, assign
arms with `sample(rep(c("Program", "Comparison"), length.out = 60))`
under seed 14003, and compare the arms' change scores with a Welch
two-sample test: the arms gain 6.4651 and 4.5033 points, a difference of
1.9618 [$-2.5867$, 6.5103], $p=.3915$. A pooled-variance or `lm()`
interval differs in the fourth decimal, so name the test. A second
baseline with an independent measurement error, used for selection but
not for the change score, removes this particular selection-on-error
artifact in the recipe; it does not by itself identify a programme effect.
The artifact also has a regression signature. On the original scales,
the fitted slope of change on baseline is
$b_{\mathrm{post,pre}}-1=r(s_{\mathrm{post}}/s_{\mathrm{pre}})-1=-0.3707$.
When each measurement is standardized separately, the corresponding
slope is $r-1=-0.3629$. These are distinct calculations; the raw-scale
slope equals $r-1$ only when the two sample SDs agree. Thus "pupils who
started lowest gained most" can arise with a zero programme effect.

::: {.callout-warning title="What regression to the mean is not"}
It is not a claim that an intervention failed, and it is not a claim
that one succeeded. In this recipe it is a consequence of two things holding
together: repeated noisy measurement of the same quantity, and
selection on an extreme value of the first measurement. Where either
is absent, this particular mechanism is absent. Where both are present, a
single-arm pre-post comparison cannot distinguish a real effect from
the artifact, whatever the p-value [@barnett2005].
:::

### Selection on the predictor and selection on the outcome




Selection on the predictor and selection on the outcome are often
discussed together and behave very differently. The recipe below is a
correctly specified linear model over the whole range: an admission-test
score predicts first-year grade point average with a true slope of 0.02

$\sim\text{Normal}(100, 15^2)$ and error SD 0.45. With seed 14006 the
full-sample slope is 0.021 (SE 0.0014, $R^2=.3091$, $r=.556$).

keeps.

Under a correctly specified linear model with errors independent of the
predictor, restricting the predictor range preserves the population slope;
sample estimates still vary. What
it destroys is precision and apparent strength. A selective institution
concluding that "the admission test barely predicts grades" from a
within-admitted correlation has confused a restricted correlation with a
weak relationship. Selecting on the outcome instead halves the slope,
because that rule removes low-outcome applicants disproportionately at
low test scores. Selection on the outcome, and attrition related to the
outcome, are threats of a different order from selection on the
predictor.

lm(gpa ~ score, data = subset(applicants, score >= 110))

### Missingness and attrition are selection by another name

The same logic covers rows that disappear rather than rows never
recruited. Three standard labels describe how missingness relates to the
data [@little2002; @littlerubin2019]. **Missing completely at random**
is unrelated to observed and unobserved values, so a complete-case
regression loses observations without systematic selection on their values.
**Missing at random** means that, conditional on the observed information,
missingness does not depend on the missing values. It can bias a
complete-case analysis, but need not do so: missing outcomes depending only
on a fully observed predictor can preserve its correctly specified
conditional regression. **Missing not at random** means that dependence on
missing values remains after conditioning on the observed information.
The observed records alone cannot identify that mechanism; analyses require
explicit assumptions and sensitivity checks. The target and the missingness
process together determine whether a complete-case result is adequate.

Two habits matter more than the labels. Report the funnel, how many
units were eligible, invited, observed, retained and analysed, with the
reason at each step; Chapters 1 and 9 built that discipline and Section
7.1 applies it to Project STAR. And resist the idea that adding
predictors repairs selection: a larger model changes what is held fixed
among the units that remain and restores none that left. Where dropout
depends on the outcome, the analytic sample is a selected-on-the-outcome
sample, and Section 4.2 shows what that does.

::: {.callout-warning title="Selection changes who is being compared"}
A regression estimates a comparison among the rows it receives. If
those rows arose through participation decisions, attrition,
eligibility cutoffs or an institution's admission rules, the estimand
quietly becomes a statement about that selected group. This is a
design and data problem. Fitting an ordinary regression to the retained
rows does not by itself repair it; explicit selection methods require
additional information and defensible assumptions.
:::

## Measurement, Aggregation, and the Unit of Analysis {#ch14-unit}

The previous sections asked which comparison was made and among whom.
This one asks what the columns actually contain and what the rows
actually are.

### Measurement error in a predictor and in a control






Chapter 7 separated the conditions of the least-squares algebra from the
requirement that a recorded predictor adequately represent the construct
the estimand names, and no residual plot assesses that requirement.
Motivation measured with a scale whose error variance is $0.75^2$ against
a true-score variance of 1 has reliability $1/(1+0.75^2)=.64$; with
seed 14008 and 800 records the slope falls from 4.8327 with the true
predictor to 3.0577 with the measured one, close to the predicted
$5\times.64=3.2$. The SE 0.1683 does not warn of this, the
residual plot cannot show it, and the p-value stays below .001: the
estimate is aimed at the wrong quantity. In this single-predictor linear
model, classical measurement error multiplies the population slope by the
predictor's reliability. With several mismeasured or correlated predictors,
bias need not be toward zero [@cohen2003; @fox2016].

The more damaging consequence appears when the mismeasured variable is a
control. Suppose a programme has no effect but socioeconomic status
causes both participation and the outcome.

Draw the four columns in the
order shown, so that the seed reproduces the printed values.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{status}_i &\sim\text{Normal}(0, 1),\\
\text{participation}_i &= 0.9\,\text{status}_i+v_i,
&& v_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 1),\\
\text{outcome}_i &= 50+0\,\text{participation}_i+3\,\text{status}_i
+\varepsilon_i,
&& \varepsilon_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 3^2),\\
\text{proxy}_i &= \text{status}_i+w_i,
&& w_i\sim\text{Normal}(0, 0.9^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

The proxy's reliability is $1/(1+0.9^2)=.5525$. With seed 14009 and 800
records, `outcome ~ participation` gives 1.3709 for a true effect of
zero, `outcome ~ participation + status` recovers $-0.113$, and
`outcome ~ participation + proxy` gives 0.7377, leaving about 54 percent
of the unadjusted bias in place. "We controlled for socioeconomic status" is
therefore an incomplete sentence: what matters is how well status was
measured [@aeraApaNcme2014]. **Construct drift** is the same problem
with a different face, since a variable named `engagement` in a 2015 and
a 2020 wave may be two constructs if the items, response scale or
administration changed. Regressions do not notice; a codebook and a
documented measurement history do.

### Ecological inference: the rows are not people






An **ecological inference** transfers a relationship estimated among
aggregates to the individuals inside them, and the two need not agree in
magnitude or in sign [@robinson1950]. The recipe makes the
disagreement exact. Sixty occupations of 40 workers vary in their share
of women, drawn Uniform(.05, .95); the occupation level is
$40-18\,\text{share}+\varepsilon$ with error SD 3; within any
occupation women earn 2 thousand dollars more than men, with worker
noise SD 4.

With seed 14010 the three numbers are $-3.0228$ at worker level pooled,
1.9869 at worker level within occupation, and $-14.3063$ [$-17.3278$,
$-11.2847$] at occupation level. Only the middle one estimates the
quantity in the recipe. The occupation-level slope, read as a gender
gap, is about seven times the true gap and points the wrong way: it is
not wrong about occupations, it is wrong about workers. The
within-occupation differences average 1.9602 and run from $-2.2702$ to
6.0976, with 90 percent positive. The worker-level pooled estimate is
negative although its rows are individuals, because the omitted
occupational structure does the work composition did in Section 3.1.
This is a reversal and the ecological fallacy in one dataset.

## Specification Sensitivity and Dependence {#ch14-sensitivity}

### Analyst degrees of freedom




Everything so far assumed one analysis. In practice a defensible
analysis has many defensible versions, and the choice among them is made
by a person who can see the results. Modest undisclosed flexibility
suffices to produce significant support for essentially any hypothesis
[@simmons2011]; the response is to run the reasonable specifications
and report the distribution rather than one selected member of it
[@steegen2016].

The Chapter 7 and 8 question supplies a natural example: how does
occupation-average income differ across occupations with different
average education? Five adjustment sets (education alone, adding
prestige, adding the percentage of women, adding both, and adding occupational type alone) and three sample rules (all 98 type-complete rows,
the 93 remaining after dropping the five largest Cook's distances from
the education-only fit, the 96 with income at or below 20 thousand) give
fifteen plausible descriptive specifications, each an `lm()` of
`income` on `education` and the set's other terms, with 95 percent
intervals from `confint()`. The education coefficient, read in thousands
of dollars per year of average education, runs from $-0.2179$ to 0.9370
with a median of 0.7301; eleven of the fifteen have $p<.05$, three are
negative, and four intervals cover zero. Reported by adjustment set,
education alone gives 0.6472 to 0.8830, adding the percentage of women
0.7301 to 0.9292, adding occupational type 0.7983 to 0.9370, and the six
specifications containing prestige collapse to $-0.2179$ to 0.3023, which
is where every interval covering zero sits. The spread is not
mysterious: education and prestige correlate
.8665 across these occupations, so models containing both split the
shared variation between them, which is the collinearity Chapter 8
examined and also a change of estimand, because the coefficient now
compares occupations at the same prestige.

A stable coefficient across fifteen models shows that the result does
not depend on those fifteen choices. It says nothing about an omitted
common cause that none of the fifteen contains, about selection that
shaped all fifteen samples identically, or about measurement error
present in every version. A robustness table is a useful disclosure;
it is not a proof of causality and not a substitute for design.
:::

### Multiplicity and the four disclosures

Chapter 4, Section 3.3, developed multiplicity: as the number of comparisons grows,
so does the chance that at least one crosses a conventional threshold
under a true null, and it calibrated a declared family. In an
applied project the comparisons are rarely counted, because they
accumulate informally across outcomes, subgroups, covariate sets,
transformations and exclusion rules. The practical response is
disclosure rather than arithmetic [@wasserstein2016; @appelbaum2018].
Four disclosures do most of the work.

::: {.callout-note title="Four disclosures"}
1. **Prespecify.** Write the primary specification and the primary
   outcome before seeing results, which separates confirmation from
   exploration.
2. **Count.** Report the number and nature of the analyses performed,
   so that a reader can calibrate the p-values.
3. **Show the set.** Present the sensitivity set rather than its best
   member, and label subgroup findings exploratory unless they were
   prespecified.
4. **Open the file.** Share code and data where permitted, which makes
   the specification auditable [@nationalAcademies2019; @peng2011;
   @nosek2018].
:::

### Dependence is a design fact {#ch14-dependence}






Every standard error in this collection assumes that rows carry
independent information, or that the calculation represents the
dependence. When pupils share a classroom, measurements repeat within a
person, or records repeat within a site, treating rows as independent
can misrepresent uncertainty. Positive classroom clustering in the examples
below makes independent-row standard errors too small; ignoring a useful
pairing can instead make them too large. Treating dependent observations as
independent replicates is **pseudoreplication**.

Project STAR is the worked case, and Chapter 9 §7 owns its mechanics, so
recall its result rather than re-deriving it. Among the 3,745
observed-reading pupils in 79 schools, kindergarten reading averaged
434.7323 in regular classes and 440.5474 in small ones, a difference of
5.8151 points. Treating pupils as independent gives an SE of 1.0377; HC3
gives 1.0416, barely different; clustering pupils within their schools
gives 1.8476, about 1.7805 times the row-level value, so with
$t_{.975,78}=1.9908$ the clustered interval is [2.1368, 9.4935] against
the row-level [3.7807, 7.8496]. Unequal spread across pupils was not the
issue addressed by the clustered calculation; it allows residual
dependence within schools while treating schools as independent. This
cluster-based approximation needs enough independent schools and a
suitable model. The within-school randomization is a separate design
fact: it neither uniquely selects this covariance estimator nor makes
the interval an exact randomization interval.

A short calibration check makes the cost of the wrong choice visible
without leaving the collection's methods. Twenty classrooms of 15
pupils, treatment assigned at classroom level with a true effect of
zero, classroom SD 6 against pupil SD 5 and therefore
$\rho_I=6^2/(6^2+5^2)=.5902$.

Draw the three random
quantities in the order shown, so that the seed reproduces the printed
values; `rbinom(20, 1, .5)` assigns each classroom independently rather
than forcing a 10-and-10 split, and each classroom's draw is repeated to
its 15 pupils.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{treat}_g &\sim\text{Bernoulli}(.5),
&&\text{repeated to the 15 pupils of classroom }g,\\
a_g &\sim\text{Normal}(0, 6^2),
&&\text{one draw per classroom},\\
\text{score}_{ig} &= 60+0\,\text{treat}_g+a_g+\varepsilon_{ig},
&& \varepsilon_{ig}\sim\text{Normal}(0, 5^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

With seed 14011 one dataset gives the same estimate 0.2343 from pupil
rows and from classroom means, the latter from `score ~ treatment` on
the 20 classroom averages, but standard errors of 1.0021 and 3.3249. One
dataset proves nothing about calibration, so repeating the same recipe
1,000 times with seed 14013 counts how often each nominal 95 percent
interval covers zero: 48.2 percent from pupil rows and 94.3 percent from
classroom means. The pupil-row analysis is not slightly optimistic; it
is wrong about the information the design supplied.

::: {.callout-warning title="Dependence is a design fact, not a modelling preference"}
An analysis does not become appropriate for clustered data because the
cluster identifier was not recorded. When treatment is assigned by
classroom, the assignment unit is the classroom and the analysis must
reflect it: analysing classroom means is the simplest honest response,
Chapter 9's cluster-robust covariance is the one used for Project
STAR, and multilevel models are the standard alternative outside this
collection. Sampling pupils within classrooms is a distinct design;
the sampling and dependence structure, not the presence of a classroom
label, determines the unit of inference.
:::

## What a Design Supplies That Adjustment Cannot {#sec-ch14-design}

### What randomization supplied in Project STAR

A causal effect compares outcomes for the same unit under two conditions.
Write $Y_i(0)$ for pupil $i$'s outcome without the programme and $Y_i(1)$
for the outcome with it. Only the outcome under the assigned condition
is observed. This notation assumes well-defined conditions and no
spillover from one pupil's assignment to another pupil's outcome.

| Pupil | Assigned condition | $Y_i(0)$ | $Y_i(1)$ |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| A | Without programme | 12 | ? |
| B | With programme | ? | 19 |
| C | Without programme | 20 | ? |
| D | With programme | ? | 16 |

: Four invented pupils: each row is missing the other potential outcome. {#tbl-ch14-counterfactual tbl-colwidths="[16,40,22,22]"}

Could any row establish its pupil's programme effect? Could the observed
group difference do so? The treated mean is 17.5 and the untreated mean
is 16, a difference of 1.5, but the groups contain different pupils.
For this constructed illustration alone, reveal the missing outcomes:
A would score 18 with the programme, B would score 15 without it, C would
score 27 with it, and D would score 11 without it. Their individual effects
are 6, 4, 7 and 5, averaging 5.5. The observed difference is not that
average in this allocation.

Randomly assigning exactly two of these four pupils, with all six pairs
equally likely, would make the unadjusted difference unbiased for their
average effect across repeated assignments; it would neither fill the missing cells nor
make every realized difference equal 5.5. A sound uncertainty calculation
represents that variation. The small table separates an individual effect,
an average effect and an observed group comparison before a fitted model
can blur them together.

Sections 2 to 6 catalogued what adjustment cannot do: remove a
confounder nobody measured, repair a mismeasured control, restore rows
that left, tell a confounder from a mediator or a collider, or decide
which comparison the question wants. A design supplies what adjustment
cannot, because it acts before the data exist.

Project STAR assigned kindergarten pupils to class types within their
schools by a known probability mechanism [@finn1990; @mosteller1995],
and that mechanism supplies three things at once.

::: {.callout-note title="What randomization supplied in Project STAR"}
1. **Independence under the assignment mechanism**, conditional on
   school and any other variables used to set allocation probabilities,
   between assignment and baseline characteristics or potential outcomes.
   This concerns measured and unmeasured characteristics and does not
   guarantee exact balance in one realized sample. On the same 3,735
   primary records, the adjusted comparison is 6.6575 (SE 1.6974,
   [3.2782, 10.0368]) and the unadjusted one 5.8955 (SE 1.8491,
   [2.2143, 9.5767]); adjustment changes precision and the fitted
   comparison without supplying the randomization warrant.
2. **Fixed timing**, so class type is settled before the kindergarten
   year and no within-year measure can be a pre-treatment common
   cause; nothing in the data would show that after the fact.
3. **A named assignment mechanism** against which uncertainty can be
   assessed. Assignment was within schools. Section 6.3's interval
   additionally treats schools as approximately independent clusters,
   allowing dependence within them. It is a cluster-asymptotic
   approximation, not an exact randomization interval or a unique
   consequence of the assignment protocol.
:::

What randomization does
not supply is equally explicit, and Chapter 9 listed it: 349 of the
4,094 eligible pupils have no recorded reading score, and their absence
is a selection question randomization does not answer; the link from
recorded class type to original assignment is unverified in the
distributed file; the raw arm means weight schools by arm-specific
counts; and the result concerns assigned class type, one kindergarten
reading outcome and participating Tennessee schools, not a realized
headcount or a portable policy dose response [@krueger1999;
@hanushek1999; @nye2000; @chetty2011].

### Four designs, named and bounded

When assignment is not available, some studies borrow an event or a rule
that behaves, under stated assumptions, like part of an assignment
mechanism. Read the vocabulary, recognize the claim and check the
assumption that carries it; the procedures are a separate course.

| Design | Identifying idea in one sentence | The assumption that carries it | What it does not remove |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Natural experiment | An external event or administrative accident allocates exposure in a way the units did not choose | The event is unrelated to the units' potential outcomes | Selection into the affected population; measurement and dependence |
| Difference in differences | Compare the change over time in an exposed group with the change in an unexposed group | The two groups' outcomes would have moved in parallel without the exposure | Differential composition change, anticipation, and other events at the same time |
| Regression discontinuity | Compare units just above and just below a threshold that determines exposure | Potential-outcome means would be continuous at the cut without the exposure; precise manipulation or another change at the same cut can undermine this | Anything away from the threshold; the estimate is local |
| Instrumental variables | Use a variable that shifts exposure but has no other route to the outcome | Relevance, independence and exclusion; a complier-effect reading also needs monotonicity and a well-defined exposure | Weak-instrument imprecision; under these conditions the effect concerns compliers |

: Four designs as reading vocabulary, with the assumption each rests on. {#tbl-ch14-designs tbl-colwidths="[18,32,26,24]"}

Chapter 1 §3.2 gave one short illustration, and recalling it fixes the
pattern. A lottery offer of a programme place changes take-up; if the
lottery is independent of the outcome and affects it only by changing
take-up, the offer can identify an effect for those whose take-up the
lottery changed. Independence and exclusion require support rather than
assertion, further assumptions decide which effect is identified and for
whom, and none of it makes the volunteers represent a wider
population.

### Where this chapter's reasoning stops

The audit is a discipline, not a method: it supplies no estimator and
cannot supply a design the study did not have.

::: {.callout-note title="Four boundaries"}
1. **No new causal estimator.** The chapter develops identification questions
   but does not implement an observational causal estimator. Recognizing that department is a
   mediator for one question and a confounder for another says what a
   regression cannot do, not what to fit instead.
2. **Dependence.** Aggregating to the cluster is honest but discards
   within-cluster information; Chapter 9's clustered covariance is the
   calculation used here, and multilevel models are the natural
   continuation outside this collection.
3. **Missing data.** They receive an audit and a bounded claim, not a
   method; multiple imputation is the continuation.
4. **Measurement error.** It is diagnosed and its direction stated,
   not corrected; errors-in-variables models are the continuation.
:::

What the
chapter does supply is transferable: naming the estimand, describing the
comparison a model computes, checking who is in it and what was
measured, disclosing how many analyses were run, and writing a final
sentence that stays inside all of it.

## From Analysis to a Credible Claim {#ch14-claim}

### Five stages for auditing a results paragraph

The chapter closes by auditing one results paragraph against five stages
and rewriting it. The paragraph concerns the generated district data of
Section 3.1, so every number can be checked and the truth is known.

The five stages are this chapter's reading device for one results
paragraph, not the collection's account of the research process, and they complement the broader schemes introduced in Chapter 1: §6.3's six quality-evaluation questions ---
Question alignment under Alignment; Evidence integrity, Justification
adequacy and Inferential adequacy under Support; Transition fidelity and
Claim calibration under Translation --- and §7.3's six-stage, two-phase
construction workflow. The workflow explains when a problem arose, while
the audit judges the completed record; the five stages group the audit
questions in @tbl-ch14-audit and replace neither scheme.

::: {.callout-note title="The five stages of this chapter's audit"}
1. **Research question:** state the substantive question and its mode.
2. **Population and unit, measurement and design:** define what one
   row represents, how variables were produced, how units entered and
   left, and what comparisons the design warrants.
3. **Estimand, data, model, and estimation:** name the target
   comparison explicitly, construct the analytic sample, specify the
   model that computes that comparison, and estimate it.
4. **Assumption checking and sensitivity, uncertainty and evidence:**
   examine mean structure, dependence, support, measurement and
   specification sensitivity, and report what moved.
5. **Interpretation, prediction, scope, and bounded claim:** write a
   conclusion whose unit, verb, population and range the previous four
   stages support.

Stage 5 is not a formatting step. Failures can originate at any
earlier stage; many computations in this chapter ran exactly as
specified, and Stage 5 is where an unresolved mismatch upstream
becomes a false sentence.
:::

### One paragraph, audited and rewritten

::: {.callout-important title="Draft results paragraph, as submitted"}
Using data on 240 pupils across four schools, we examined the effect
of supplementary tutoring on reading achievement. A regression of
end-of-year reading score on weekly tutoring hours showed that each
additional hour of tutoring raised scores by 6.5784 points
($p<.0001$), explaining 72 percent of the variance in achievement. The
effect was highly significant, confirming that tutoring is an
effective intervention. Because the relationship was so strong, we
recommend that the district expand tutoring to 10 hours per week for
all pupils, which the model predicts would produce scores of
approximately 89 points. Robustness checks confirmed the finding.
:::

Every number in that paragraph is arithmetically correct, and the
paragraph is indefensible at four of the five stages.

**Stage 1.** The paragraph uses causal verbs, "effect", "raised",
"effective intervention", for an observational regression with no
assignment mechanism and no identification argument. The mode changed
silently between the analysis and the sentence: the analysis supports
an associational claim and the sentence makes a causal one.

**Stage 2.** One row is a pupil in one of four fixed schools, not
sampled at random, differing systematically in tutoring provision and
baseline achievement. Nothing is said about how tutoring was
allocated, which Section 3.1 showed to be decisive, about who was
measured with what instrument, or about pupils missing an end-of-year
score.

**Stage 3.** The fitted model is `score ~ hours`, whose coefficient is
the pooled comparison. That is a legitimate estimand, but not the one
the sentence describes: 87 percent of the predictor variation lies
between schools, so the reported number is largely a comparison of
school averages, and the within-school comparison $-2.0018$ has the
opposite sign.

**Stage 4.** "Highly significant" is offered as confirmation, but a
small p-value states compatibility with a null model, not size,
importance or causal status [@wasserstein2016]; "explaining 72
percent of the variance" is an algebraic decomposition of sample
variation; and "robustness checks confirmed the finding" names neither
the checks, nor their number, nor their spread. The intervals suit
this recipe's independent residual errors conditional on four fixed
schools, which a real report would have to justify rather than infer
from a missing cluster column.

**Stage 5.** The recommended prediction is made at 10 tutoring hours
per week, and the observed range is 0.1496 to 7.5722 hours, with no
pupil at or above 8. The pooled model returns 88.9215 points there and
the school-adjusted model returns 57.5615 at School 4: outside the
support the two fits of the same data separate by more than 31 points
because nothing constrains them. The recommendation also assumes the
association would survive an intervention that changes how tutoring is
allocated, which is precisely what the design cannot license.

\Needspace{34\baselineskip}

::: {.callout-tip title="Revised results paragraph"}
We analysed end-of-year reading scores and weekly tutoring hours for
240 pupils in four schools in one district. Tutoring is allocated by
schools rather than assigned by the study, so every estimate below is
a comparison, not an effect. Pooling across schools, pupils receiving
one more hour of tutoring per week scored 6.5784 points higher on
average (95 percent interval [6.0565, 7.1003]). This pooled figure
mainly reflects differences between schools: only 12.79 percent of the
variation in tutoring hours occurs within schools, and
better-resourced schools both provide more tutoring and have higher
average scores. Within schools the comparison reverses: adjusting for
school, pupils receiving one more hour scored 2.0018 points lower
(95 percent interval [$-2.8533$, $-1.1504$]), all four school-specific
slopes were negative, from $-2.6281$ to $-1.2688$, and a
school-by-hours product block did not improve fit ($F(3,232)=0.4345$,
$p=.7285$). Leaving out any one school left the adjusted comparison
between $-2.2289$ and $-1.7504$. The negative within-school pattern is
consistent with tutoring being allocated to pupils who are already
struggling, and these data cannot separate that allocation from any
benefit of tutoring itself. The intervals are model-based and
appropriate for independent residual errors conditional on four fixed
schools; real school data would require a residual-dependence check.
Observed tutoring ranges from 0.1496 to 7.5722 hours per week, so we
make no statement about ten-hour provision. Answering the district's
actual question would require either random assignment of tutoring or
an explicit identification argument with adequate pre-allocation
measurements and defensible assumptions about confounding, support and
measurement. Baseline achievement would be relevant evidence, not a
guarantee by itself.
:::

The revision reports more numbers than the original, retracts the causal
verb, names the estimand each number belongs to, states the support
limit, discloses the dependence question, and ends by saying what design
would answer the question. It is a weaker claim and a stronger piece of
research.

**[lower, upper]**), holding **[conditioning set]** fixed. This is a

the **[alternative estimand]** comparison gives **[value]**, and the

## Reading Bridge

A credible claim is an aligned one: the question, the estimand, the
design, the rows, the fitted comparison and the final sentence must
describe the same thing. Adjustment is a decision about an assumed
structure, helpful for a pre-treatment common cause and harmful for a
mediator or a collider, and a coefficient that moves is not a
diagnosis. A pooled slope is a composition-weighted average of a
within-group and a between-group slope, so a reversal is arithmetic
about weights rather than a paradox, and Berkeley's pooled,
conditional and standardized comparisons are three answers to three
questions. Selection, restriction, attrition and regression to the
mean change who is compared before any model runs; measurement error
and aggregation change what a column and a row mean; fifteen
defensible specifications can spread an estimate across zero; and
dependence follows the design, as Project STAR's clustered interval
showed. Randomization supplies a known allocation mechanism: conditional on
its allocation variables, assignment is independent of pre-treatment
attributes in the randomization distribution. It also fixes timing and
defines repetitions for design-based inference; a cluster-based model
interval remains an approximation. The
quasi-experimental designs are named so that you can read them. Carry
the five-stage audit and the claim template into your own project,
where the first question is not which model to fit but which
comparison the question asks for. Part Two turns to measurement
itself, where the constructs this chapter asked you to audit become
the objects modelled.

## Key terms {.unnumbered}

Use this reference to revisit the concepts introduced here. The Part One
Concept Reference gives the broader reference and the principal home of
each concept.

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning or essential distinction |
|:--|:--|
| Directed acyclic graph (causal diagram; DAG) | A diagram whose arrows state assumed direct causes and whose directed paths cannot return to their starting point; it records assumptions that can be questioned, rather than conclusions produced by the data. |
| Mediator (intermediate variable) | A variable caused by the focal predictor and lying on a path to the outcome; one kind of post-treatment variable, not a synonym for every variable measured after treatment. Conditioning on it changes a total-effect comparison; a direct causal reading needs additional identification and modelling conditions. |
| Collider (common effect) | A variable caused by two others. A path through a collider is blocked unless the collider or a descendant is conditioned on; such conditioning can induce an association along that path. |
| Adjustment set | The variables conditioned on for a stated estimand under an assumed structure, justified by that structure and the timing rather than by the available columns or a coefficient's movement. |
| Aggregation reversal (Simpson's paradox; strict Simpson reversal) | A sign difference between a pooled comparison and the stratified or standardized comparisons, strict when every stratum points the opposite way to the pooled result; it arises from composition, not from a computational error. |
| Within-group, between-group, and pooled comparison | Three estimands from one dataset: inside a level of the grouping variable, across group summaries, and across all rows ignoring the grouping, with the pooled slope a weighted average of the other two by the within and between shares of predictor variation. |
| Direct standardization (standardized comparison) | Recomputing each group's summary under one declared common distribution of a stratifying variable; a third estimand rather than a compromise between the pooled and conditional comparisons. |
| Range restriction (restriction of range) | Keeping only part of the observed range; restricting the predictor under a correctly specified linear model costs precision, apparent strength and support outside the window, while restricting on the outcome also moves the slope. |
| Missingness mechanisms (MCAR; MAR; MNAR) | MCAR means missingness is unrelated to observed and missing values; MAR means it is unrelated to missing values conditional on observed information; MNAR means dependence on missing values remains. Complete-case validity depends on the target and mechanism, and MNAR requires assumptions not identified by the observed data alone. |
| Attenuation from measurement error | In a single-predictor linear model, classical predictor error multiplies the population slope by reliability. With several predictors the direction can differ; a mismeasured control can leave residual confounding. |
| Ecological inference (ecological fallacy) | Inferring an individual-level relationship from aggregate records. Aggregate and individual relationships can differ in sign and magnitude; the aggregate relationship alone does not identify the individual comparison. |
| Specification sensitivity (multiverse analysis; analyst degrees of freedom) | The spread of an estimate across the defensible analyses that could have been run; a disclosure about specification, not evidence about an omitted common cause, selection or measurement shared by every version. |
| Pseudoreplication (dependence as a design fact) | Treating dependent observations as independent replicates, misrepresenting uncertainty. The relevant dependence, sampling and assignment structure must be represented; its effect on a standard error depends on the comparison. |
| Identification argument (design warrant) | The explicit reasons a comparison estimates the intended causal quantity, whether assignment or a named quasi-experimental design with its stated assumption; naming a design is not meeting its assumption. |
| Bounded regression claim (credible-claim template) | A concluding statement whose unit, verb, conditioning set, supported range, design and disclosed sensitivity all match the analysis that produced it. |

## Appendix A: Composition Arithmetic {.unnumbered}

### How the pooled slope splits {.unnumbered}

The decomposition in Section 3.2 follows by separating a pupil's deviation
from the district mean into a deviation from the school mean and the
school mean's deviation from the district mean:

$$x_{ig}-\bar x=(x_{ig}-\bar x_g)+(\bar x_g-\bar x).$$

Squaring and summing gives a within term, a between term and a cross-term.
Within each school, $\sum_{i\in g}(x_{ig}-\bar x_g)=0$, so the cross-term
vanishes. The same argument for the product of the $x$ and $y$
deviations gives

$$
S_{xx}=S_{xx}^{W}+S_{xx}^{B},\qquad
S_{xy}=S_{xy}^{W}+S_{xy}^{B}.
$$

Divide by $S_{xx}$ and multiply each component by its own denominator:

$$
\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=
\frac{S_{xx}^{W}}{S_{xx}}\frac{S_{xy}^{W}}{S_{xx}^{W}}+
\frac{S_{xx}^{B}}{S_{xx}}\frac{S_{xy}^{B}}{S_{xx}^{B}}.
$$

The two ratios at the right are the common within-school slope and the
between-school slope weighted by school size. Because this example has
60 pupils in every school, ordinary regression on the four school means
gives that same between-school slope. With unequal school sizes, the
between-school fit for this identity must weight each school by its size.
The weights displayed as .1279 and .8721 combine slopes displayed as
$-2.0018$ and 7.8372 to recover 6.5784 from the full-precision values.
Rounded ingredients can give a slightly different last digit.

The identity explains the source of a pooled coefficient; it does not
establish that one component has a causal interpretation. Nor does
reducing the between-school weight alone guarantee a smaller pooled
slope: the between-school slope can change at the same time.

### Standardization changes the weights {.unnumbered}

For gender $a$ and department $d$, let $p_{ad}$ be the admission rate and
$q_{ad}$ the share of that gender's applications sent to the department.
The observed pooled rate is

$$p_a=\sum_d q_{ad}p_{ad}.$$

Choose one declared set of weights $q_d$ that sums to one. The standardized
rate is $p_a^*=\sum_d q_dp_{ad}$, so the contrast becomes

$$p_{\mathrm{women}}^*-p_{\mathrm{men}}^*
=\sum_d q_d(p_{\mathrm{women},d}-p_{\mathrm{men},d}).$$

Using each department's share of all 4,526 decisions gives 42.9955 percent
for women and 38.7319 percent for men. The 4.2637-point difference concerns
that common distribution. It is a rate difference, not the conditional
odds ratio from a logistic model; changing the scale and changing the
weights are separate decisions.

### The change-score identity {.unnumbered}

Let $X$ be pretest and $Y$ posttest on their original scales. The fitted
slope from regressing change $Y-X$ on $X$ is exactly

$$
b_{Y-X,X}
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y-X)}{s_X^2}
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{s_X^2}-1
=r\frac{s_Y}{s_X}-1=b_{Y,X}-1.
$$

In the generated records it is $-0.3707$. If both measurements are first
standardized separately, their SDs are one and the corresponding slope
is $r-1=-0.3629$. The raw-scale expression reduces to $r-1$ only when the
two sample SDs agree. In the generating population of Section 4.1 they
are equal, so the population change slope is $\rho-1=.64-1=-0.36$.
Sampling variation need not preserve equality of the two sample SDs.

### Reliability changes the apparent gain {.unnumbered}

Keep the 400 stable abilities and the seed 14002 recipe, but change both
measurement-error SDs together to 2, 6 or 10. Select the lowest 15 percent
separately in each version. The error variance increases while the true
ability variance stays at $8^2$, so reliability decreases. Every
programme effect remains zero.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

| Error SD | Reliability | Observed correlation | Apparent gain | Paired $p$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2 | .9412 | .9385 | 1.0570 | .0082 |
| 6 | .6400 | .6371 | 5.4842 | < .0001 |
| 10 | .3902 | .3952 | 13.1818 | < .0001 |

: Less reliable selection produces a larger apparent gain in this recipe. {#tbl-ch14-reliability tbl-colwidths="[15,20,23,22,20]"}

The lower reliability gives unusually low measurement errors a larger
role in who enters the selected group. Repeating the measurement does
not repeat those errors, and the selected group rises further. The
p-values test zero mean change among selected records; they cannot
convert that change into a programme effect.

### Repeated sampling checks an interval procedure {.unnumbered}

For the classroom recipe in Section 6.3, each of 1,000 repetitions
draws 20 classroom assignments, 20 classroom offsets and 300 pupil
errors, in that order, under seed 14013. Each repetition fits the
pupil-row regression and the regression on 20 classroom means, then
records whether its 95 percent interval covers the true effect zero.
With equal classroom sizes and classroom-level assignment, aggregation
leaves the estimated contrast unchanged but represents the independent
units in its standard error.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

| Calculation | Unit treated as independent | Coverage in 1,000 repetitions |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Pupil-row regression | 300 pupils | 48.2% |
| Classroom-mean regression | 20 classrooms | 94.3% |

: Interval coverage under the declared classroom recipe. {#tbl-ch14-coverage tbl-colwidths="[34,34,32]"}

Coverage is a property of repeated intervals under a specified
data-generating process. It cannot be read off a single interval, and
these results do not certify either procedure under every possible
classroom process. Here the classroom-mean interval has the usual
Normal linear-model justification conditional on nondegenerate
classroom assignments. The pupil-row calculation ignores the common
offset and counts information repeatedly.
